questions.q: An agent signs a contract with a third party "as agent for" the principal. Who are the parties to that contract?
choices: The agent and the third party
The principal and the third party
The agent, principal and third party
questions.explain: The agent isn't normally a party; the contract binds the principal and the third party.

questions.q: What is the warranty of authority?
choices: The principal's promise to pay the agent's fee
The agent's implied promise they have authority
A brokerage's guarantee of all its licensees
A seller's written warranty about the property
questions.explain: Dealing with third parties, an agent impliedly promises they're acting within their authority. Breach makes them personally liable.

questions.q: Before 1994, who did the licensee working with a buyer legally represent?
questions.explain: Under seller sub-agency, all duties ran to the seller, though buyers often assumed otherwise.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · How real estate agency evolved in BC

questions.q: When did designated agency come into force in BC?
questions.explain: June 2012. Dual agency was then banned in 2018.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · How real estate agency evolved in BC

questions.q: Under designated agency, who owes the client full agency duties?
questions.explain: Only the designated licensee(s) are the client's agents; the brokerage still supervises and protects confidences (s.32).

questions.q: Which is NOT a duty of a brokerage offering designated agency under Rules s.32?
choices: Sharing client files among all its licensees
questions.explain: s.32 requires supervision, confidentiality and even-handed treatment.

questions.q: Which brokerages must still use brokerage agency?
choices: Brokerages with fewer than five licensees
Those doing only rental and/or strata management
Brokerages that work only in remote areas
Brokerages that handle only commercial deals
questions.explain: Brokerage agency is the only model allowed for rental-only or strata-management-only brokerages.

questions.q: Which is NOT dual agency?
choices: One licensee acting for buyer and seller in one trade
Two designated agents at one brokerage acting for opposite sides
One licensee acting for two buyers wanting the same property
One licensee acting for both landlord and tenant
questions.explain: Different designated agents in the same brokerage acting for each side isn't dual agency.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · The ban on dual agency

questions.q: An unrepresented buyer at your open house asks you, the seller's designated agent, to represent them. Which is NOT an option?
choices: Another designated agent at your brokerage
You representing both buyer and seller
Hiring a licensee at another brokerage
questions.explain: Acting for both would be prohibited dual agency.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · The ban on dual agency

questions.q: Which report led to the 2018 ban on dual agency?
choices: The Expert Panel on Money Laundering
questions.explain: The Independent Advisory Group's 2016 report found dual agents can't be fully loyal or keep both sides' confidences.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · The ban on dual agency

questions.q: What must be true for the s.64 dual agency exception to apply?
choices: The parties are related to each other
questions.explain: All three elements must be met; consent alone isn't enough. "Impracticable" means not capable of being done.

questions.q: Who must sign the Disclosure of Risks Associated with Dual Agency form?
questions.explain: The managing broker signs and explains how each element is met; copies go to BCFSA.

questions.q: Which form is a BCFSA prescribed form that can't be altered?
choices: The standard Contract of Purchase and Sale
questions.explain: DORTS is prescribed (s.54). The others are BCREA standard forms.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · Standard forms: prescribed vs other

questions.q: Which BCFSA disclosure form is optional, as long as the required content is given?
choices: Disclosure of Risks to Unrepresented Parties (s.55)
Disclosure to Sellers of Expected Remuneration (s.57)
questions.explain: The s.56 form is non-mandatory; the others are prescribed.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · Standard forms: prescribed vs other

questions.q: In Travelers Guarantee v. Farajollahi, a father had his 14-year-old daughter sign a loan for him. Was he bound?
choices: No, minors can't act as agents
Yes, a minor can be an agent
Only if a witness was present
questions.explain: Anyone of sound mind can be an agent, because the agent isn't a party to the principal's contract.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · Who can be an agent?

questions.q: Under Rules s.43, which agreement must be in writing (unless the client waives it)?
choices: A service agreement with an owner/seller
A referral fee agreement with another agent
An agreement with a cooperating brokerage
questions.explain: s.43 requires a written service agreement for owners/sellers; buyer agreements are prudent but not required by s.43.

questions.q: Under Rules s.44, when must the client get a copy of the service agreement?
questions.explain: Give each client (each co-owner) a copy immediately.

questions.q: Under a standard exclusive right to sell listing, the owner finds their own buyer during the term. Is commission payable?
choices: No, the brokerage didn't find the buyer
Yes, on any sale during the term
Only if the buyer saw the MLS® listing
questions.explain: An exclusive right to sell pays commission on any sale during the term. Only a true "exclusive listing" amended to exempt the owner changes that.

questions.q: Under an open listing, who earns the commission?
choices: Only the brokerage that's the effective cause
The first brokerage to sign a listing with them
The brokerage with the highest commission rate
questions.explain: Only the effective cause is paid. An owner's own sale pays nobody and ends all the listings.

questions.q: Which action with an unrepresented buyer most risks creating an implied agency?
choices: Advising them what price to offer
Presenting their offer to the seller
questions.explain: Advising or negotiating for them, or revealing your client's secrets, crosses the line into implied agency.

questions.q: Which is NOT required for agency by estoppel?
choices: A change of position by the third party
questions.explain: Estoppel arises from the principal's words or conduct; no written agreement is needed.

questions.q: A licensee acts without authority, and the principal later refuses to ratify. Who may be liable?
questions.explain: Without ratification the principal isn't bound, and the agent may be liable for breach of warranty of authority.

questions.q: Holding an open house when the listing only says "show the property" is an example of what?
questions.explain: Implied authority covers what's necessary and incidental to the express authority (and open houses are also customary).
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · How much authority does the agent have?

questions.q: Which type of authority arises from the principal's conduct toward a third party, rather than from the agency agreement?
questions.explain: Apparent authority is based on estoppel: what a reasonable third party believes from the principal's conduct.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · How much authority does the agent have?

questions.q: Your client is overseas and asks you to sign a contract amendment for them. What do you need first?
choices: Their verbal instruction over the phone
Nothing, the listing agreement is enough
questions.explain: The listing or buyer agency agreement doesn't authorize signing. Get separate written authority, then sign your own name "as agent for" the client.

questions.q: A licensee copied a client's signature onto an addendum without written authority. What was the result?
choices: No penalty, since the client agreed
questions.explain: 7-day suspension plus $750 enforcement expenses.

questions.q: Which ends an agency relationship by operation of law?
choices: The seller firing the agent by email
questions.explain: Death, mental incapacity or bankruptcy of either side ends agency by operation of law.

questions.q: Which is NOT a way the Multiple Listing Contract (s.14) ends?
choices: The seller receiving a low offer
questions.explain: It ends on expiry, mutual written agreement, completed sale, licence suspension or cancellation, brokerage bankruptcy, or a s.65 conflict.

questions.q: Al buys land in his own name for Sam without disclosing Sam's role. Sam goes bankrupt. Who can the seller sue?
questions.explain: With an undisclosed agency, the third party can sue the agent (or the principal once revealed).
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · The agent and third parties

questions.q: A seller tells their agent to hide a leaky basement, and the agent tells a buyer there are no leaks. Who can the buyer sue?
choices: Both the agent and the seller
questions.explain: The agent is personally liable for fraud ("my client told me" is no defence), and the principal is liable too.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · The agent and third parties

questions.q: Which duty requires a seller's agent to advise whether an offer is the best reasonably obtainable?
choices: The duty of confidentiality to the client
The duty of reasonable care and skill
The duty to obey lawful instructions
questions.explain: In tort, a competent agent seeks fair market value and advises on offers.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · Tort duty: reasonable care and skill

questions.q: An agent hands a listing to a colleague without the client's permission. Which duty is breached?
choices: The duty to account for money
The duty of honesty to all
questions.explain: The client chose that agent; work can't be delegated without permission (standard forms allow a replacement in limited cases).
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · Agency duty: do it yourself

questions.q: A client sues alleging breach of fiduciary duty. Who bears the burden of proof?
questions.explain: In fiduciary claims, the agent must show they met their duties.

questions.q: Which fiduciary duty continues after the agency relationship ends?
questions.explain: Most duties end with the relationship, but confidentiality continues indefinitely.

questions.q: Under Galambos v. Perez, when does a conflict of interest exist?
choices: Whenever an agent is paid by commission
A substantial risk of material, adverse effect
Only when the agent owns the property in question
Only if the client actually complains about it
questions.explain: A substantial risk that representation will be materially and adversely affected by the agent's interests or duties to others.

questions.q: Two of your buyer clients want to make offers on the same property. Under Rules s.65, what are your options?
choices: Represent both and stay strictly neutral
Stop for both, or keep one with both signing
Keep whichever client called you first
Let the sellers pick which buyer you keep
questions.explain: Stop acting for both, or continue for one only if both sign the Agreement Regarding Conflict of Interest Between Clients.

questions.q: When is the Agreement Regarding Conflict of Interest Between Clients signed?
choices: In advance, at the start of the agency
questions.explain: It must be signed when the conflict arises, not in advance.

questions.q: What does the Released Client keep under a s.65 agreement?
choices: A right to veto the other's offer
questions.explain: The Released Client gets no further advice, but you still can't disclose their confidential information.

questions.q: Your buyer client wants to see one of your own listings. What does BCFSA allow?
choices: Nothing; you must refer the buyer elsewhere
Showing it and giving facts, after disclosure
Writing an offer while acting for both sides
Advising the buyer on what price to offer
questions.explain: You can show it and give general factual information after disclosing the conflict. An offer or advice triggers s.65.

questions.q: What does "be a conduit, not a filter" mean?
choices: Share only good news with clients
questions.explain: Don't decide for the client what's important. When in doubt, disclose.

questions.q: In Baillie v. Charman, what did the agent have to pay after steering the property to a friend at $270,000?
choices: Only the commission on this one sale
Nothing, because the friend paid fair value
questions.explain: The property was resold for $317,000. Breach of fiduciary duty: both commissions plus the profit.

questions.q: In Ocean City Realty, a licensee secretly agreed to share commission with the buyer. What did the brokerage lose?
questions.explain: The seller wasn't told, so the brokerage forfeited the entire commission.

questions.q: After a listing expired, the former agent emailed buyers that the sellers would take far less than appraisal. What was breached?
choices: Nothing, because the agency had ended
Only the s.57 remuneration disclosure rule
The duty of personal performance to them
questions.explain: Confidentiality survives the relationship: 7-day suspension, $1,000 expenses and a remedial course.

questions.q: A seller tells you about an unpermitted basement suite and says "don't tell buyers." What must you do?
choices: Keep it confidential, as a fiduciary
Disclose it, or stop acting if refused
Tell only buyers who ask about it
questions.explain: It's a material latent defect under s.59; confidentiality doesn't override it. If the seller insists, stop acting.

questions.q: A seller says "don't show the home to families with young children." How should you respond?
choices: Follow it, since the seller decides
Follow it for this listing only
Ask the managing broker to show it
questions.explain: Only lawful instructions are obeyed. Family status is a protected ground; if the seller insists, stop acting.

questions.q: Which Rules section requires licensees to act honestly toward everyone, clients and non-clients alike?
questions.explain: s.33: honesty. s.34: reasonable care and skill.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · The Rules: s.30, s.33, s.34

questions.q: A licensee copied 2,097 sq ft from an old listing; the home was really 1,672 sq ft. Which Rule was breached?
choices: s.33, the duty of honesty to all
s.53 disclosure of interest in trade
questions.explain: Reprimand, remedial course and $1,250 expenses under s.34.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · The Rules: s.30, s.33, s.34

questions.q: Under RESA s.4, who can't sue for remuneration?
choices: Someone unlicensed when services were given
A brokerage on an open listing
A licensee paid by a cooperating brokerage
questions.explain: You must have been licensed (or exempt) when providing the services.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · The principal's duties to the agent

questions.q: A buyer introduced during the listing buys 45 days after it expires. Is commission payable under the standard MLC?
questions.explain: Commission is payable if the buyer was introduced during the term and the contract is made within 60 days after expiry.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · The principal's duties to the agent

questions.q: A buyer validly rescinds under the HBRP. Is commission payable under the standard listing?
choices: Yes, because the contract was signed
No, not under the standard listing
Yes, paid out of the 0.25% fee
questions.explain: The Multiple Listing Contract says no commission is payable when the buyer rescinds under the HBRP.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · The principal's duties to the agent

questions.q: Who is legally entitled to the commission under a listing contract?
questions.explain: The brokerage signed the contract. RESA s.7: licensees accept pay only from their own brokerage.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · The principal's duties to the agent

questions.q: A seller agrees to pay the licensee whatever the price exceeds $375,000. What's wrong?
choices: Nothing, as long as it's in writing
It must first be filed with BCFSA
It needs the buyer's written consent
questions.explain: Net listings are prohibited. The licensee was reprimanded, fined $5,000, sent on a course and paid $1,250 expenses.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · The principal's duties to the agent

questions.q: An Alberta licensee refers a buyer to you. Can your brokerage pay them a referral fee?
choices: Yes, out-of-province licensees can be paid
Only if they first become licensed in BC
Only by routing it through the buyer
questions.explain: s.66 bars paying people who should be licensed, but out-of-province licensees are an exception.
questions.ref: Lesson 9 · The principal's duties to the agent

questions.q: When is a DORTS NOT required?
choices: At a listing presentation to an owner
Hosting an open house, without discussing needs
Before writing an offer for a buyer client
Before you start representing a new seller
questions.explain: The open-house and general-question exceptions apply only if you don't ask about or receive motivation, finances or needs.

questions.q: You give a listing presentation but don't get the listing. Did you need a DORTS?
choices: Yes, give one and keep a copy
Only if the owner signed it
questions.explain: You'll hear the owner's motivations, so give it; the brokerage keeps a record (s.83).

questions.q: What are the purposes of the Disclosure of Risks to Unrepresented Parties form?
choices: To create a limited agency with that party
Explain risks, limit services, urge representation
To set the commission the unrepresented party pays
To replace parts of the contract of purchase and sale
questions.explain: It explains you're loyal to your client, lists the limited services you can offer, and encourages getting their own agent.

questions.q: A home inspector pays you $100 per referral. When must you disclose it to your client?
choices: Only if the client asks you
questions.explain: Disclose source and amount promptly when recommending (s.56), and give your honest opinion of the inspector.

questions.q: A developer tells you, after several sales, that you've earned a bonus. What must you do?
choices: Nothing, since the bonus is already earned
Give s.56 disclosure to each client involved
Return the bonus to the developer at once
Disclose it to BCFSA, not to the clients
questions.explain: Go back and give s.56 disclosure to each client whose purchase counted. A potential bonus is disclosed up front under s.30(f).

questions.q: When must the seller's licensee give the s.57 Disclosure to Sellers of Expected Remuneration?
choices: Only if the buyer is unrepresented
questions.explain: With each offer, in dollars: gross, co-op share, net to the listing brokerage, and any other remuneration.

questions.q: Commission is 7% on the first $100,000 and 3.5% on the balance. What's the gross on $745,000?
Why does s.57 matter most when one offer comes from an unrepresented buyer?
choices: The seller pays no commission then
questions.explain: With no cooperating brokerage, the listing brokerage keeps the whole commission, a conflict the seller should see in dollars.

questions.q: Which person is an "associate" for Rules s.53?
questions.explain: Associates include your spouse, a trust or estate you benefit from substantially, and a corporation where you or your spouse hold 5%+.

questions.q: When must the Disclosure of Interest in Trade be delivered?
choices: Only if the other side asks
questions.explain: Before any agreement. Late disclosure has led to discipline, and Compar v. Foss shows the contract may be voidable.

questions.q: Why is buying a client's property through your own company especially risky?
choices: The HBRP doesn't apply to such purchases
Title can't be registered in a company name
questions.explain: The Indemnity Plan excludes claims where the insured has an ownership interest.
